lightning.notes: The ceiling is the RECEPTACLE, not the truck. 30A at 240V is 7.2 kW, whatever Pro Power Onboard is rated for in total. Corrected from 9600 W, which was the truck's figure and overstated what this connection can actually deliver.

l1430-ext.name: L14-30 generator extension cord
l1430-ext.ends: Standard generator extension: MALE plug on one end, FEMALE connector on the other.
l1430-ext.howItConnects: The male plug goes into the source's L14-30 output (the F3800+ or the truck). The female connector twists onto the male pins of the inlet box at the panel. Ordinary cord, ordinary directions - nothing improvised.
l1430-ext.notes: One cable serves both panels. This is what closes the old male-to-male worry: the house side is a MALE inlet, so a normal cord fits, and there are no exposed live pins at either end.

breakerPlatform.notes: Leviton load centers use proprietary plug-on LB-series breakers. Hot and neutral conductors land on panel lugs, not on the breaker itself. Not interchangeable with Square D / Eaton / Siemens breakers.

suffixKey.-T: current-generation standard thermal-magnetic (supersedes the un-suffixed LBxxx hydraulic-magnetic parts)
suffixKey.-S / -ST: Smart (1st gen / 2nd gen) metering + remote trip

smartUpgradePath.notes: 2nd-gen smart breakers are the drop-in metering replacements for the standard -T parts in these same slots. The catalog suffix is -0ST, not -ST: every one of these strings is what the installed hardware reports through the LWHEM-2 cloud (verified 2026-08-22 for all seven ratings except 25A/60A, which this house does not use). 22 of the 32 devices in this file are now these parts.

A.name: Panel A
A.notes: Primary backup panel - can be powered by Anker F3800+

mainBreaker.notes: Face is marked only 'LEVITON 200'. LM200-T is thermal-magnetic; LM200 is the older hydraulic-magnetic part. All branch breakers in this panel are thermal-magnetic '-T' style, so LM200-T is the likely part. Confirm from the side label or panel schedule.

generatorInlet.interlockType: mechanical sliding-plate interlock over the top two right-column positions

connection.location: Wall, immediately left of Panel A (garage, interior)
connection.deviceType: flanged power inlet box - MALE pins, not a receptacle
connection.notes: RESOLVED. Earlier this was read off a photo as a female receptacle, which implied a male-to-male cord - it does not. It is a male flanged power inlet, so an ordinary L14-30 extension cord connects it to the Anker with no exposed live pins. The PBN30 model number is the owner's recollection and is the one part still worth confirming; the male gender is verified.

generatorInlet.notes: Slots 2 and 4 are NOT a branch circuit - they are the backup feed. The interlock plate physically prevents the main and this breaker from both being ON.

B.name: Panel B
B.notes: Secondary panel - can be powered by the F-150 Lightning through the outdoor 30A/240V inlet, which caps it at 7.2 kW. 14 of 30 slots are empty, so there is real room for smart-breaker or solar expansion - but count on fewer than 14. Slots 5 and 7 sit opposite the feed-through lug at 6/8, and the 2/0 feeder conductors landing there most likely make that pair unusable. Check before planning around them.

mainBreaker.notes: Face is marked only 'LEVITON 200', same as Panel A. Confirm LM200-T vs LM200.

connection.notes: Same arrangement as Panel A and the same cord fits both, so this is a male inlet - that much is verified by the owner. Still not photographed: the exact NEMA configuration is inferred from the PBN30 (L14-30) and from the fact that one cable serves both panels. Confirm on sight before the first real transfer.

generatorInlet.notes:
Slots 2 and 4 are the backup feed, not a branch circuit. Confirmed from photo and the directory card ('GEN INPUT').
The truck side is the Lightning's 240V 30A outlet, which is what caps this panel at 7.2 kW regardless of Pro Power Onboard's total rating. Confirm the truck-side outlet configuration when you confirm the inlet.

devices.label: Leviton energy monitor (LWHEM-2)

equipment.description: Load center energy monitor for Panel A - the hub the smart breakers report through, and the source of every Leviton reading in the energycap pipeline

circuits.notes: 5 W is an order-of-magnitude estimate for a metering gateway, not a nameplate reading. It is recorded as a real small figure rather than 0 W so the breaker does not read as untraced, and it is noise against either backup source's ceiling.

notes: DO NOT SHED, and it is not in any shed list. This breaker powers the Leviton LWHEM-2 energy monitor - the gateway every smart breaker in this panel reports through. Switching it off does NOT de-energise anything else: the smart breakers are ordinary mechanical breakers and keep carrying current. What you lose is all metering, the app, and remote on/off for this panel, which is exactly the visibility you want during an outage.

One monitor per panel, each on its own breaker: Panel A's is on A-27-29, Panel B's on B-17-19. They are separate devices with separate hub ids, which is why a panel's smart breakers go dark independently of the other panel's.
Unlike the feed-through lug at B 6/8, this IS a breaker with a handle. There is something to switch here; the instruction is simply not to.

CORRECTED 2026-08-22. This was recorded as the Siemens whole-house SPD on the owner's earlier identification, and the Leviton app's own name for it - 'Smart Home' - is what raised the doubt. The Siemens unit was external and fed from here; it is gone, replaced by the plug-on LSPD1-T now at 22/24, and these slots became the monitor's supply.

monitoring.reason: The monitor's own supply comes through a dumb breaker, and nothing upstream of it is metered, so the one load in the house that can never appear in the data is the metering system itself.
monitoring.instrumentationPath: None worth building. It is a few watts, and swapping this breaker for a smart one would put the monitor's supply through a breaker that needs the monitor to report.

hardware.breakerType: plug-on Type 1 surge protective device with two independent 15 A single-pole thermal-magnetic branch breakers in one body
hardware.notes: Installed 2026-08-22 in place of the two separate 1-pole 15 A LB115-T breakers that were in slots 22 and 24. ONE PHYSICAL BODY HOLDS BOTH BREAKERS AND THE SPD: A-22 and A-24 are still two devices here because they still switch and trip independently, which is what the panel reader needs, but pulling the unit removes both circuits and the panel's surge protection together. Ratings are Leviton's published spec (Type 1, 25 kA surge, 10 kA SCCR, 10 kA nominal discharge); the body has not been photographed. There is no smart variant, so smartReplacement is deliberately absent.

devices.label: Master bath + closet lights
notes: This breaker lives in the Leviton LSPD1-T at 22/24, which is also the whole-panel surge protective device. The circuits it feeds did not change when it went in on 2026-08-22.

SWITCHING IT OFF DOES NOT DISABLE SURGE PROTECTION. Leviton's spec is explicit that the SPD is fed line-side and 'surge protection continues, even if the breaker is off, or tripped'. So these two circuits can be shed like any others without giving up protection - which is not true of the older arrangement, where an external SPD sat behind its own breaker.
PULLING THE UNIT is the thing to think twice about: it takes out both circuits and the surge protection at once, and it is the only surge protection Panel A has now.
Status is on the unit's own LEDs, not in this app: green = protected, red = protection gone, replace the unit, off = no power. Worth a look when you are at the panel anyway.

monitoring.reason: Leviton makes no smart/metering version of the LSPD1-T, so these two circuits are the only branch circuits in Panel A that cannot report usage - the other 18 devices all do. It is a combination device: metering them means giving up the panel's surge protection or finding the SPD another two slots, and Panel A has none free.
monitoring.instrumentationPath: A CT on each of the two branch conductors, or accept the gap - these are lights and a vent fan, about 770 W of connected load between them.

It feeds the HVAC heat-strip subpanel at the air handler (2/0 aluminum, roughly 135A at 75C). The only disconnecting means for those loads is inside that subpanel.
Its downstream load (20 kW of electric heat) IS counted in the Panel B load figure, but it can never be shed at Panel B.

It probably explains the phantom 'Oven' the directory card lists at 5/7. Those slots face this lug, and the 2/0 feeder conductors landing here most likely make the pair unusable - so a breaker that was written on the card was never installed there. Treat 5/7 as doubtful when planning expansion.

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION, 2026-08-22: in the Leviton app the owner labelled the placeholder object occupying these two positions 'Heat Strip Subpanel'. That is a second, separately recorded statement that 6/8 feeds the HVAC subpanel and not a branch circuit.

DELIBERATELY NOT SHED. The Panel B outage procedure is heat-pump-only: lock the electric heat out at the Evolution Connex control and let the heat pump run. Shedding this breaker would turn off the one piece of heating that fits inside a 7.2 kW inlet.
40A 2-pole confirmed from photo. No load figure recorded, so it contributes 0 W to the Panel B load meter - see hvac-heat-pump-on-truck before assuming it fits.
A 'Mud Room Air Conditioner' is also recorded on Panel A 23/25 (20A 2-pole). That is a separate unit or a wrong label; this one is the main system.

METERED as of 2026-08-22. The LB240-0ST smart breaker on these slots reports this circuit's real draw every 30 seconds (1,350 W observed with the compressor at part capacity), so the 0 W above - the last untraced load in the house, and the reason the Panel B meter reads LOW - can be replaced with a measured figure once a few days of heating and cooling have been recorded. Do not guess it from this one sample: a variable-speed 5-ton unit at part capacity is nothing like its peak.

circuits.notes: A single dedicated plug. 1000 W is a placeholder: the F3800+ AC charge rate is set in the Anker app and can run from a couple of hundred watts to about 1800 W. Record the rate you actually use.

equipment.description: Load center energy monitor for Panel B - the hub the smart breakers report through, and the source of every Leviton reading in the energycap pipeline

circuits.notes: 5 W is an order-of-magnitude estimate for a metering gateway, not a nameplate reading. It is recorded as a real small figure rather than 0 W so the breaker does not read as untraced, and it is noise against either backup source's ceiling.

notes: DO NOT SHED, and it is not in any shed list. This breaker powers the Leviton LWHEM-2 energy monitor - the gateway every smart breaker in this panel reports through. Switching it off does NOT de-energise anything else: the smart breakers are ordinary mechanical breakers and keep carrying current. What you lose is all metering, the app, and remote on/off for this panel, which is exactly the visibility you want during an outage.

One monitor per panel, each on its own breaker: Panel A's is on A-27-29, Panel B's on B-17-19. They are separate devices with separate hub ids, which is why a panel's smart breakers go dark independently of the other panel's.
Unlike the feed-through lug at B 6/8, this IS a breaker with a handle. There is something to switch here; the instruction is simply not to.

These two slots were previously recorded as VERIFIED EMPTY from the panel photo, and the Leviton app's placeholder object here is what raised the contradiction. Owner-resolved 2026-08-22: the breaker is real, so Panel B has one fewer available pair than the empty-slot count used to imply.

monitoring.reason: The monitor's own supply comes through a dumb breaker, and nothing upstream of it is metered, so the one load in the house that can never appear in the data is the metering system itself.
monitoring.instrumentationPath: None worth building. It is a few watts, and swapping this breaker for a smart one would put the monitor's supply through a breaker that needs the monitor to report.

subpanels.name: HVAC heat-strip subpanel
subpanels.locationDetail: Mounted on the air handler itself, NOT in the garage with panels A and B. A sweep of Panel B does not go anywhere near it.
subpanels.disconnectArrangement: No main breaker. Three 50A 2-pole handles, a six-disconnect arrangement - those handles ARE the disconnecting means for everything here.

feeder.notes: Confirmed aluminum, 2/0 - the copper-vs-aluminium question is settled. Whether the run satisfies the NEC 10-ft tap rule is NOT settled: it needs a measured run length and confirmation of whether it is in raceway. No code conclusion has been recorded either way.

monitoring.reason: Loads here never pass through a Panel B branch breaker, so no Leviton LWHEM smart breaker can ever measure them. Swapping breakers in Panel B will not instrument this branch, no matter how many are swapped.
monitoring.instrumentationPath: A CT pair on the 2/0 aluminum feeder is the only way to meter this.

appliances.notes: ONE heat kit, not three. The three 50A 2-pole breakers are the field power circuits of a single 20 kW appliance - roughly 6,667 W per circuit. Never sum them as three 20 kW loads.

Likely fed from one of the three subpanel circuits, but which one is unknown and even the fact that it is fed from here is unconfirmed. No draw figure recorded, so it contributes nothing to the total below.

20 kW of connected electric heat against a 7.2 kW inlet is roughly 2.8x the ceiling. The heat strips must be locked out at the Evolution Connex control before any transfer.
DO NOT switch off all three handles as a blanket move: the blower is probably on one of them, and killing the blower leaves the heat pump unable to run at all.

truckHome.name: Full Power Mode
truckHome.description: Truck is home - use both Anker (Panel A) and Lightning (Panel B)
truckHome.notes: Both panels can be energized. Panel A is still limited by the Anker's 3800 W output, so the Panel A shed list applies. Panel B is limited by the 30A/240V outdoor receptacle - 7.2 kW, not the truck's 9.6 kW - and 20 kW of electric heat sits behind a feed-through lug that NO Panel B breaker can switch off. Lock the heat strips out at the Evolution Connex control and run heat-pump-only; the Panel B shed list (cooktop, oven) does not touch them.

truckAway.name: Conservation Mode
truckAway.description: Truck is away - Anker only (Panel A)
truckAway.notes: Only 3.8 kWh available. Prioritize refrigerators, sump pump, ejector pump and internet. Avoid washer, dishwasher and high-draw appliances. The three orange-taped breakers (1/3 dryer, 10/12 kitchen + dishwasher, 19/21 water heater) are the shed list the tape was marking. Note A-10-12 is common trip: shedding it also kills slot 12.

openQuestions.recorded: Three 50A 2-pole breakers in the HVAC subpanel, all treated as heat-strip circuits
openQuestions.observed: One of the three likely also feeds the FE4ANB006L00 fan coil blower
openQuestions.resolution: SAFETY-RELEVANT. Until this is identified, do NOT switch off all three subpanel handles: killing the blower leaves the heat pump unable to run, so the outage move that was supposed to save power removes your heat entirely. Identify the blower circuit, then the procedure becomes 'switch off only the two strip-only handles'. Until then, lock heat out at the Evolution Connex control instead.

openQuestions.recorded: 2/0 aluminum feeder, roughly 135A at 75C, tapped off the Panel B bus with no overcurrent device
openQuestions.observed: Conductor material and size confirmed; run length and raceway status unknown
openQuestions.resolution: The copper-vs-aluminium question is RESOLVED: it is 2/0 aluminum. What is not resolved is whether this unfused tap satisfies the NEC 10-ft tap rule - that needs a measured run length and confirmation of whether the run is in raceway. No code conclusion has been recorded either way, and none should be quoted from this file until it is measured. Everything downstream is protected only by the Panel B 200A main.

openQuestions.recorded: Three 50A 2-pole breakers serving one KFCEH3301C20 heat kit
openQuestions.observed: The kit may be wired for two field power circuits rather than three
openQuestions.resolution: Confirm the number of field power circuits from the kit's wiring diagram. If it is two, the third 50A handle feeds something that is currently unaccounted for. The 20 kW total does not change either way - it is one appliance, roughly 6,667 W per circuit across three, and must never be summed as three 20 kW loads.

openQuestions.recorded: Panel B outage plan is heat-pump-only on a 7.2 kW inlet
openQuestions.observed: No running-watt or starting-draw figure is recorded for the 5-ton 284ANV060000
openQuestions.resolution: Heat-pump-only is the right plan - 20 kW of strips against 7.2 kW is not a plan at all - but nobody has checked that the heat pump itself fits. Record the unit's running watts and locked-rotor draw from the nameplate. A variable-speed Evolution unit should soft-start, but that is an assumption, not a measurement. B-10-12 is deliberately NOT on the shed list because of this plan; if the figures come back too high, that decision has to be revisited.

openQuestions.recorded: Panel B connected load computes from recorded circuits only
openQuestions.observed: The 40A heat pump outdoor unit still has no load figure recorded
openQuestions.resolution: Nearly closed. The 20 kW HVAC heat kit behind the 6/8 feed-through lug is now counted, B-26 is the Anker trickle-charge plug, and B-28-30 is an SPD that genuinely draws nothing. The only real gap left is B-10-12, the 5-ton heat pump outdoor unit - and it is the one thing the outage plan intends to RUN, so its figure matters. See hvac-heat-pump-on-truck.

openQuestions.recorded: Male L14-30 flanged inlet, Reliance Controls PBN30, same as Panel A
openQuestions.observed: Never photographed; the description is carried over from Panel A and from the fact that one cord serves both
openQuestions.resolution: The gender is verified by the owner - it is a male inlet, so the male-to-male worry is gone here too. What is still inferred rather than seen is the exact NEMA configuration and the model. Photograph it, and confirm the truck-side outlet configuration at the same time.

openQuestions.recorded: Endpoints recorded on one leg of two confirmed MWBCs
openQuestions.observed: A-5-7 has endpoints on slot 7 only; A-10-12 on slot 10 only
openQuestions.resolution: Every Panel A breaker now has an identity, and the MWBCs are confirmed. What is left is that each of these two handles has a second 120V leg with nothing recorded on it. Turning the handle off still kills both legs - that part is not in doubt - but there are outlets somewhere fed from slots 5 and 12 that nobody has followed. The four entries in unassignedEndpoints are the obvious candidates.

openQuestions.recorded: Handwritten directory cards in both panels
openQuestions.observed: The Panel B card lists an oven at 5/7 (empty slots - the real oven is at 14/16), a washer at 11 (the walkthrough puts it on A-9), 'Furn' at 6/8 (which is a feed-through lug, not a furnace breaker), and has no entry for slot 26 (the Anker trickle-charge plug)
openQuestions.resolution: Every entry on the card is now accounted for, so this is purely a reprint job. The 'Furn' label at 6/8 is the dangerous one: it implies a handle that can turn the heating off, and there is no handle there at all. Both cards should be reprinted from this data - `npm run insert`.

openQuestions.recorded: Water heater at 4500 W, mini-split at 1200 W
openQuestions.observed: Both figures are class estimates, not nameplate readings
openQuestions.resolution: Both devices are now correctly identified, but neither number came off a label. Read the water heater's element rating from the tank and the mini-split's MCA and maximum fuse size from the outdoor unit. Both are shed in every scenario, so the remaining-load figure does not move either way - this only affects how much shedding them buys you.

safetyWarnings.title: Disconnect Trickle Charger
safetyWarnings.message: BEFORE starting: Unplug the Anker F3800+ from its 120V trickle charge outlet. That outlet is the dedicated plug on Panel B slot 26, not a Panel A circuit.

safetyWarnings.title: No Panel B Breaker Turns Off the Heat Strips
safetyWarnings.message: 20 kW of electric heat is fed through a lug at Panel B 6/8 - a bus tap with no handle. Switching off every breaker in Panel B leaves it live. Lock electric heat out at the Bryant Evolution Connex control (SYSTXBBECC01-B) and run heat-pump-only. The only physical disconnect is the three 50A handles inside the subpanel at the HVAC air handler.

safetyWarnings.title: Main Breaker First
safetyWarnings.message: Always turn OFF the main breaker BEFORE engaging the generator/backup inlet breaker.

safetyWarnings.title: Interlock Safety
safetyWarnings.message: The interlock prevents the main breaker and generator inlet from being ON simultaneously. Never attempt to bypass this.

safetyWarnings.title: 2-Pole Breakers Are Common Trip
safetyWarnings.message: Slots 5/7, 10/12, 13/15, 19/21, 23/25 and 27/29 in Panel A each share one handle. Switching one slot off switches both. Plan shed lists by device, not by slot number.

panelA.title: Unplug Anker Trickle Charger
panelA.instruction: Locate the Anker F3800+ and unplug it from the 120V wall outlet it uses for trickle charging.
panelA.warning: This must be done BEFORE connecting to the panel.

panelA.title: Turn Off High-Draw Breakers
panelA.instruction: At Panel A, turn OFF these breakers to prevent overloading the Anker:

panelA.title: Turn Off Main Breaker
panelA.instruction: Flip the MAIN breaker at Panel A to the OFF position.
panelA.warning: This disconnects your home from the grid.

panelA.title: Connect Anker to Panel
panelA.instruction: Use the L14-30 extension cord. Its MALE plug goes into the Anker F3800+ L14-30 output; its FEMALE end twists onto the inlet box on the wall immediately left of Panel A. The inlet has male pins, so the cord only fits one way round.

panelA.title: Engage Generator Inlet Breaker
panelA.instruction: Slide the interlock plate and flip the 30A 2-pole generator inlet breaker (Panel A slots 2/4, top of the right column) to ON. The interlock should now allow this since the main is OFF.

panelA.title: Turn On Anker
panelA.instruction: Power on the Anker F3800+. Panel A circuits (except those turned off) should now have power.

panelA.title: Verify Critical Loads
panelA.instruction: Check that the refrigerator, sump pump, and internet are working.

panelB.title: Position the Truck
panelB.instruction: Park the F-150 Lightning near the outdoor 30A receptacle.

panelB.title: Lock Out Electric Heat at the Thermostat
panelB.instruction: At the Bryant Evolution Connex control (SYSTXBBECC01-B), lock out auxiliary / emergency electric heat so the system runs heat-pump-only. Do this FIRST - it is the only way to keep 20 kW of heat strips from calling for power.
panelB.warning: No breaker in Panel B can disconnect the heat strips. They are fed through a lug at slots 6/8 that has no handle. The thermostat lockout is your primary control.

panelB.title: Turn Off High-Draw Breakers
panelB.instruction: At Panel B, turn OFF these breakers:
panelB.warning: Do NOT switch off the heat pump outdoor unit at 10/12 - heat-pump-only is the plan, and that is the breaker feeding it. Slots 2/4 are the GENERATOR INLET, not the double oven; leave them available. Slots 6/8 are a feed-through lug with no handle; there is nothing there to switch.

panelB.title: Physical Backstop: Kill the Strip-Only Circuits
panelB.instruction: Go to the HVAC subpanel mounted at the air handler - NOT in the garage with Panels A and B. It is an older grey load center with three 50A 2-pole breakers and no main. Once you know which of the three feeds the blower, switch off ONLY the other two.
panelB.warning: Do not switch off all three. The fan coil blower is probably on one of them, and without the blower the heat pump cannot run either. Until the blower circuit is identified (see hvac-blower-circuit), rely on the thermostat lockout from step 2 and leave these alone.

panelB.title: Turn Off Main Breaker
panelB.instruction: Flip the MAIN breaker at Panel B to the OFF position.

panelB.title: Connect Truck to the Inlet
panelB.instruction: Same L14-30 extension cord as Panel A. Its MALE plug goes into the truck's bed-mounted 240V 30A outlet; its FEMALE end twists onto the outdoor inlet box.
panelB.warning: The outdoor inlet has not been photographed yet. It should be the same male L14-30 inlet as Panel A - check it fits before you need it to.

panelB.title: Enable Pro Power Onboard
panelB.instruction: In the truck, enable Pro Power Onboard and select the appropriate output level.
panelB.warning: The 30A/240V receptacle caps this at 7.2 kW no matter what the truck can deliver.

panelB.title: Engage Generator Inlet Breaker
panelB.instruction: Flip the generator inlet breaker at Panel B to ON.
panelB.warning: Slots 2/4, top of the right column, under the interlock plate. The outdoor receptacle configuration is not yet confirmed - check it before the first real transfer.

panelB.title: Verify Panel B Loads
panelB.instruction: Check that Panel B circuits are receiving power, and watch the truck's output. If it trips or sags, electric heat is the first thing to suspect - confirm the Connex lockout held.

rechargeAnkerFromTruck.title: Check Anker Battery Level
rechargeAnkerFromTruck.instruction: If the Anker F3800+ is running low, you can recharge it from the Lightning.

rechargeAnkerFromTruck.title: Connect Charging Cable
rechargeAnkerFromTruck.instruction: Connect a charging cable from one of the truck's outlets to the Anker's AC input. If Panel B is already energized from the truck, the Anker's usual trickle-charge plug (Panel B slot 26) is live and does the same job with no extra cable.

rechargeAnkerFromTruck.title: Monitor Charging
rechargeAnkerFromTruck.instruction: The Anker can charge while also providing backup power (pass-through charging).
rechargeAnkerFromTruck.warning: The truck is now carrying Panel B AND, through the Anker, Panel A. Everything still has to fit inside the 7.2 kW receptacle ceiling.

metadata.notes: Device-first schema. One entry per physical breaker; circuits nest underneath. Shed lists live on devices via shedIn so common-trip behaviour is explicit and there is one source of truth. Not every device is a breaker: role 'feedThrough' is a bus tap with no overcurrent protection, and what it feeds lives in subpanels[]. Handwritten panel directory cards are historical, not authoritative.

changelog.summary: Owner resolved both questions v2.7 raised. Each panel's Leviton LWHEM-2 energy monitor sits on its own 2-pole dumb breaker: Panel B on a 15 A breaker at 17/19 - so those slots are NOT empty and the panel reconciles again at 18 occupied + 12 empty - and Panel A on the reused 20 A LB220-T at 27/29, which was NOT the Siemens SPD it had been recorded as. Leviton's own 'Smart Home' label for 27/29 was right. Both monitor breakers are DO NOT SHED, and the reason is not the obvious one: switching one off de-energises nothing, because smart breakers are ordinary mechanical breakers, but it takes out all metering, the app and remote control for that panel. It also means the one load in the house that can never be measured is the metering system itself. Panel A's surge protection is now a plug-on Leviton LSPD1-T at 22/24, which is a COMBINATION device - two independent 15 A single-pole breakers plus a Type 1 SPD in one body - so A-22 and A-24 keep their identities, their ten circuits and their ~770 W unchanged; only their hardware record changed. Per Leviton's spec the SPD is fed line-side and keeps protecting with those breakers off or tripped, which is a real improvement on the external Siemens unit it replaced (Panel B keeps its own Siemens SPD at 28/30). The one coverage consequence: no smart LSPD1-T exists, so A-22 and A-24 are the only Panel A branch circuits that can never report usage.

Smart-breaker retrofit. 22 of the 32 devices are now Leviton 2nd-gen smart breakers (-0ST), up from 2: 18 of Panel A's 22 devices and 4 in Panel B. Every catalog number, amp rating and pole count in this change is the installed hardware's own report through the LWHEM-2 cloud, cross-checked against the amps and poles already recorded here - all 22 agreed, so no rating changed. Each retrofitted device gains a monitoring block naming the hub, position and channel_id it is metered under, which is the join the energycap pipeline uses to inherit its label from this file. Two consequences worth knowing: B-10-12, the 5-ton heat pump and the last untraced load in the house, is now metered, so the Panel B load meter's 'reads LOW' warning can finally be closed with a measured figure; and B-26 measures the Anker trickle-charge rate that was a 1,000 W placeholder. Two new medium open questions came out of the same data - a monitor module apparently at Panel B 17/19 (so those slots are no longer claimed verified-empty) and a conflicting name on Panel A 27/29. Leviton's own label for Panel B 6/8, 'Heat Strip Subpanel', independently corroborates the feed-through finding.

Two more findings closed by owner confirmation. A-mwbc-overlap resolved: slots 5/7, 10/12 and 13/15 in Panel A are genuinely multi-wire branch circuits - two 120V legs sharing a neutral under one common-trip handle, not 240V loads - so circuitType drops 'probable'. What survives from that finding is narrower and now lives in A-unmapped: A-5-7 and A-10-12 each have a second leg (slots 5 and 12) with no endpoints recorded. B-2-4-oven resolved: the double oven is confirmed at 14/16, and the directory card's second 'Oven' at 5/7 is simply wrong. Likely cause recorded on B-6-8 - slots 5/7 face the feed-through lug and the 2/0 feeder conductors probably make that pair unusable, which also means Panel B has fewer than 14 genuinely available slots for expansion.

Both generator inlets verified by the owner as MALE flanged power inlets (Reliance Controls PBN30, model per recollection), connected with an ordinary L14-30 generator extension cord. This resolves A-inlet-receptacle, the high-severity worry that the Panel A inlet was a female receptacle needing a male-to-male cord - the photo was misread. Renamed generatorInlet.receptacle to generatorInlet.connection, because calling a male inlet a 'receptacle' is what caused the misreading in the first place. Added a top-level cables{} keyed like backupSources, referenced by generatorInlet.cable, so the one cord is described once and both panels point at it. Connection steps in both walkthroughs now say which end goes where. What remains open is only that the Panel B inlet has never been photographed (B-inlet-unphotographed, low).

Owner identification closed out every unidentified breaker in Panel A and both in Panel B. A-19-21 is the water heater (4500W, shed in both scenarios), A-23-25 is a Pioneer CYB012GMFILCAD-16 12k mini-split in the mud room addition (1200W, not the recorded 3500W - the breaker was right and the figure was wrong), A-27-29 and B-28-30 are both Siemens whole-house SPDs, B-26 is the dedicated plug that trickle-charges the Anker F3800+. The orange tape is confirmed to mean 'shut this off in an outage', so A-10-12 joins A-1-3 and A-19-21 in being shed in BOTH scenarios rather than only truck-away. SPDs carry an explicit 0W circuit so they read as 'nothing to trace' instead of inflating the untraced-capacity warning.
